slides.text: A function can hand a value back to the code that called it. Its type goes after the parameters, behind an arrow `->`. With no arrow, the function hands back nothing.
The value is the last expression of the body, with no semicolon. A call is an expression too, so it can sit in a `let`, inside `println!` or in a bigger calculation.
slides.code:
let twice = double(4);
let more = double(4) + 1;

exercises.guide: Write a function that hands back a number, then use that number.

chunks.guide: `area` takes two numbers and gives back an `i32`. The last line is the value it returns.

notes.text: The type of the value the function hands back.
No semicolon: this line is the returned value.

notes.text: True or false: this is what the caller gets.

exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `bonus(score)` is replaced by the value it returns, 8 (integer division). Then 1 is added, so it prints 9.

exercises.title: Make it return 8
exercises.guide: The function should hand back 8. Which change does it?
options: Write `2 * n;` with the factors swapped
exercises.explanation: The semicolon turns `n * 2` into a statement, so the body gives no value. Without it, `n * 2` is the last expression and becomes the returned value.

slides.text: With no `->`, a function returns `()`, the unit value: an empty tuple, with nothing in it to use. Functions that only print are of this kind.
A function returns one value, but it can be a tuple. The caller unpacks it with a `let` pattern.
An `if`/`else` is an expression, so it can be the last thing in a function. Each branch gives the value, with no semicolon.

exercises.title: Split a bill
exercises.guide: Return two numbers at once, packed in a tuple, and unpack them in `main`.

chunks.guide: The tuple type lists what comes back: the share of each person and the coins left over.

notes.text: Two values come back packed in one tuple.

chunks.guide: Unpack the tuple into two variables and print them.
chunks.text:
let (each, left) = divide(17, 5);
    println!("{} each, {} left", each, left);
